title: The Contact Group Plan: 51/49 and the Isolation of Pale
content:
The Contact Group — comprising the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, and Germany — presented its peace plan to the warring parties in July 1994. The proposal represented the most serious attempt at a negotiated settlement since the failed Vance-Owen Peace Plan of early 1993, and it introduced the territorial formula that would ultimately underpin the Dayton Agreement: a 51-49 percent division of Bosnian territory between the newly established Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska.

The plan emerged from a diplomatic context reshaped by the Washington Agreement of March 1994. With the Bosniak-Croat conflict ended and a joint Federation established, the international community could present a simplified two-entity model. The Federation would receive 51 percent of Bosnia's territory, the Republika Srpska 49 percent. The specific map drawn by the Contact Group required significant Bosnian Serb territorial concessions from the approximately 70 percent of Bosnia that VRS forces controlled at the time. For the Bosnian government in Sarajevo, the plan demanded acceptance of a Serb entity within Bosnia — a bitter concession given the ethnic cleansing through which that entity had been carved out.

The plan was presented on a take-it-or-leave-it basis. The Contact Group insisted that no amendments or counter-proposals would be entertained. This rigidity was deliberate, designed to prevent the kind of prolonged negotiation-as-delay that had characterized earlier peace processes. The Bosnian government, under heavy international pressure and recognizing that the Federation's military position was not yet strong enough to recover territory by force, accepted the plan. Croatia endorsed it. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under Slobodan Milošević also signaled acceptance, increasingly willing to distance Belgrade from the Bosnian Serb leadership.

The Bosnian Serb Assembly, however, rejected the plan. Meeting in Pale in late July and again in August 1994, the assembly voted against acceptance, unwilling to relinquish territory that the VRS held on the ground. Karadžić and the Pale leadership calculated that the international community lacked the will to enforce the plan militarily, and that time remained on their side. The rejection was decisive and repeated — a referendum organized among Bosnian Serbs produced an overwhelming vote against the Contact Group map.

The consequences of rejection were significant but slow to materialize. Milošević, furious at what he regarded as Pale's reckless defiance, imposed a partial blockade on the Republika Srpska, restricting the flow of supplies across the Drina River from Serbia proper. This blockade, while imperfect and often circumvented, represented a genuine rupture between Belgrade and Pale. International monitors were deployed along the Serbia-Bosnia border to verify compliance. The Bosnian Serb entity found itself increasingly isolated — cut off from its patron state, facing a unified Federation with growing international support, and confronting the possibility that the military balance was beginning to shift.

Yet the Contact Group Plan also exposed the limits of diplomacy without enforcement. The plan contained no mechanism for implementation against a party that refused to accept it. The international community proved unwilling to impose the settlement by force in the summer of 1994. It would take another year of war — including the fall of Srebrenica, the Markale marketplace massacre, and Operation Storm — before the military and political conditions existed for a settlement to be imposed. The 51-49 formula survived, but only after the battlefield had been reshaped to match the map that diplomacy alone could not deliver.
